extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy (Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics Book X for what counts as Pleasure, how Pleasures differ, and what constitutes Happiness (the human good). Focuses on relations among faculties, activities, virtue, and the contemplative life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not a Movement or a Generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure cannot be properly called a Movement or a Generation because movements have duration, parts, and relative swiftness/slowness, whereas Pleasure is a 'whole' complete at any given moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: acts of sight are complete at an instant (no further duration completes their nature); movements require a time-span to be complete and have distinguishable parts (e.g., building a house). Pleasure resembles an act complete at a moment, so labels like 'Movement' or 'Generation' are inapplicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not merely a supply for a previous lack
rubrics_metrics.description: The view that Pain is a lack and Pleasure the supplying of that lack fails because many Pleasures (e.g., intellectual pleasures, certain smells, sounds, memories, hopes) arise not from supply after lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mathematical study pleasures and many sensory pleasures occur without any prior 'lack' to be supplied, so Pleasure cannot be reduced to mere replenishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disgraceful pleasures are not truly pleasant (relative to character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures that arise from vicious or depraved tastes are not genuinely pleasant except to the ill-disposed; what pleases a corrupted person should not be counted a real Pleasure in the full sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: sick people's senses mislead (something white to an ophthalmia patient may not be truly white). Thus we should not generalize such tastes as genuinely pleasant for human good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some Pleasures are choiceworthy in themselves, others not
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every kind of pleasure is choiceworthy; some are choiceworthy 'in themselves' (linked to excellent activities), others are not (e.g., bodily amusements chosen for further ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness must be among things chosen for their own sakes and self-sufficient; amusements and mere bodily pastimes, even if pleasant, are not ends and so do not constitute true Happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasures differ in kind according to their source (proper pleasures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures are specific to the kinds of Workings (activities/faculties) that produce them: intellectual pleasures differ from sensory ones; within senses, pleasures differ (sight, hearing, smell, taste); animals have pleasures proper to their natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the pleasure of the musical man presupposes being musical; honourable pleasures differ from disgraceful ones; an ass prefers hay to gold. Proper pleasures perfect their corresponding activities and can hinder other different activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure perfects the act of Working
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is attendant upon the exercise of each percipient faculty and is most perfect when the faculty (in its best state) works upon the best object; Pleasure 'perfects' Working as a supervening finish (like bloom in prime).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleasure increases the accuracy and endurance of activities (geometers who take pleasure in geometry become more exact). Pleasure is not the same kind of cause as the faculty or object, but it accompanies and completes the excellent working.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper pleasures increase their associated workings; foreign pleasures hinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures proper to a given activity enhance and prolong that activity, whereas pleasures foreign to it mar or destroy the Working (and can have effects similar to Pains regarding that Working).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: those who take pleasure in flute-music cannot attend to discourse when they hear a flute; foreign pleasures can push out attention from other activities; foreign pleasures may act like pains for a given activity by destroying the working.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is intimately connected with the activity and not separable in time/nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasures attendant on Workings are closer to the Working than mere desires; they are temporally and natively intertwined with the activity, sometimes making it seem identical with the activity, though Pleasure is not itself an intellectual operation or faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This closeness explains why Pleasure might be mistaken for the working itself; nevertheless, Pleasure is distinct though inseparable in experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure is not continuous due to human faculties' limits and habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Human faculties cannot exert themselves without interruption, and repeated engagement dulls the Pleasure (novelty arouses faculties at full tension; later the act becomes careless and Pleasure is dulled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why continuous Pleasure is not possible; initial heightened attention produces pleasure that diminishes with habituation or fatigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is an activity (Working) in accordance with Excellence (Virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is not merely a state but an activity of a kind — specifically, Working in the way of Excellence; such activities are chosen for their own sake and are self-sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Workings differ (some are for other ends), Happiness must be among those chosen for their own sakes and self-sufficient. Moral actions done for excellence count toward human Happiness only insofar as they are activities in accordance with virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: The highest Happiness is contemplative activity (life of the intellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfect Happiness is the activity of the best Principle (intellect) in accordance with its proper excellence — i.e., contemplative or intellectual speculation — because the intellect is the highest internal principle, most continuous, self-sufficient, and most pleasant in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: contemplative life is continuous (we can contemplate more continuously than we can act), relatively self-sufficient (can be done alone), and akin to the life of the gods; scientific/intellectual pursuits contain pure and lasting pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical/moral virtues require external goods and social context
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical virtues (justice, liberality, courage, etc.) depend on social circumstances and require some external goods (money for liberality, power/opportunity for bravery) to be fully exercised; thus moral Happiness needs some external goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a liberal man needs money to act liberally; the brave man needs opportunities for brave action; perfection of virtuous action often requires external conditions and more numerous requirements than contemplative activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest and amusement are not ultimate ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Rest and amusement are chosen with a view to further action (rest for working again), so they cannot be the final End/Happiness; Happiness must be an end chosen for its own sake and self-sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: to toil and endure all one's life for the sake of amusement is absurd; rest is instrumentally adopted to enable further Working, not as the final end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness must be self-sufficient, complete, and of sufficient duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is self-sufficient (lacking nothing) and is not merely a passive state (one cannot be happy by merely vegetating); for perfect Happiness, a complete duration of life is required so that no point of Happiness is incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: to judge someone happy we consider the whole life and its activities; temporary or partial pleasures/pastimes do not amount to full Happiness.
